story.title: Gâteau battu, the Vimeu's own brioche
story.p1: In Quesnoy-le-Montant, between Abbeville and the Bay of the Somme, the Fréville family has been baking gâteau battu since 1956. Charles started it, his son Francis took over in 1981, and his children run the house today.
story.p2: It is a tall, fluted brioche, made with a great many egg yolks and plenty of butter, beaten for a long time before it is baked in its mould. The crumb is yellow, stringy, almost melting. Picardy serves it at weddings and christenings, at breakfast, or simply because it's there.
story.p3: The flour comes from a mill a few kilometres from Quesnoy, the eggs from Huppy, the butter from the region. No preservatives, and still it keeps for about ten days.

items.q: How far ahead should I order?
items.a: Allow 48 hours for a gâteau battu, a mini platter or a king cake. For a large order or a celebration (wedding, christening), call us a week ahead.

items.q: What sizes of gâteau battu do you make?
items.a: Several, from a small cake for two or three to a large battu for a full table. We will give you the current sizes and prices by phone or in the shop.

items.q: How do I keep a gâteau battu?
items.a: In its wrapping, at room temperature, away from heat. It keeps for about ten days. If it dries out a little, a few seconds in the oven brings it back.
Gâteau battu contains gluten, eggs and milk. Our pastries may contain nuts. Mention any allergy in your order and we will tell you what is possible.

battu.metaTitle: Gâteau battu from the Vimeu in Amiens | Maison Fréville
battu.metaDescription: What is gâteau battu, Picardy's brioche from the Vimeu? Origins, how it's made, how to keep it, and where to buy it in Amiens: Maison Fréville, 6 rue des Vergeaux.
battu.title: Gâteau battu from the Vimeu
battu.lead: A brioche as tall as a chef's hat, with a yellow, stringy crumb. Where it comes from, how it's made, and where to find it in Amiens.

sections.title: What is gâteau battu?
sections.text: Gâteau battu (literally “beaten cake”) is a traditional brioche from Picardy, born in the Vimeu and Ponthieu around Abbeville. You know it by its shape: tall, round, fluted on the sides, with a domed golden top. The dough holds a great many egg yolks and plenty of butter, which gives it that yellow colour and a very soft crumb.

sections.title: Why “beaten”?
sections.text: Because the dough is beaten for a long time, by hand in the old days, in a mixer now, until it is elastic and full of air. It then rises in a tall fluted mould before baking. The hard part is getting the same cake every day: the workshop's temperature, the humidity, the flour and the eggs all change with the seasons.

sections.title: Maison Fréville's gâteau battu
sections.text: The house has been making it since 1956 in Quesnoy-le-Montant, a Vimeu village a few kilometres from Abbeville. Founded by Charles Fréville and taken over by his son Francis in 1981, it is still run by the family. The flour comes from a nearby mill, the eggs from Huppy, the butter from the region. Since 2022 you can also find it in central Amiens, on rue des Vergeaux.

sections.title: How to eat it
sections.text: Plain, in thick slices, for breakfast or with afternoon tea. Lightly toasted with salted butter or jam. At Picardy celebrations it also goes with foie gras or dessert. In mini size it becomes a rum baba, a Nutella-filled treat or a savoury goat's cheese bite.

sections.title: Keeping it
sections.text: With no preservatives, it keeps for about ten days in its wrapping at room temperature. Don't put it in the fridge: the crumb hardens. If it starts to dry, a few seconds in the oven bring back its softness.

sections.title: Where to buy gâteau battu in Amiens
sections.text: At Maison Fréville – Les spécialités de Quesnoy-le-Montant, 6 rue des Vergeaux, near Place Gambetta and a five-minute walk from the cathedral. Open Tuesday to Saturday. For a large battu or several cakes, order 48 hours ahead.
